title: Establish Security Foundations and Governance
objective: Design governance for multi-account environments, secure deployments, and continuous compliance evaluation.

sections.title: Making the account the boundary for governance and responsibility
paragraphs: In an organization, accounts are treated not merely as billing units but as boundaries that separate environments, data classifications, operational responsibilities, and the scope of incidents. Organizations design organizational policies, delegated administrators, centralized log aggregation, shared identities, root user protection, and break-glass procedures.

Even when using AWS Organizations and Control Tower, organizations verify which operations are prohibited across the organization, which operations are delegated to individual accounts, how exceptions are approved, and how existing environments are migrated. The goal is not to introduce governance for its own sake, but to continue necessary business operations safely.

sources.label: SCS-C03 Exam Guide: Security Foundations and Governance

sections.title: Integrating Security into the Deployment Process
paragraphs: Secure deployments validate the source, dependencies, artifacts, IaC, execution roles, environment promotion, and post-deployment configuration. Rather than discovering vulnerabilities or policy violations after production, detect them as early in the process as possible, and establish approval and expiration dates for exceptions.

Continuously evaluate differences between templates and real environments, public-access settings, encryption, logs, and tags. Allowing changes that failed inspection to pass unconditionally is a loss of governance, not emergency response.

sources.label: SCS-C03 Exam Guide: Consistent Deployment Strategies

sections.title: Continuously assess compliance with evidence
paragraphs: Compliance assessments link the resources in scope, the desired state, evaluation rules, exceptions, expiration dates, owners, and remediation results. They use configuration history and operational history—not only the current configuration—to trace when a deviation occurred and whose change caused it.

Do not run automated remediation merely to reduce the number of findings. Define the target and scope of effect, execution role, stop conditions, rollback, and post-remediation reevaluation so that approved exceptions are not disrupted.

checkpoints.prompt: An organization operating production environments for multiple business units wants to separate each unit’s responsibilities while applying company-wide security controls. Which design is most appropriate?

choices.text: Separate accounts as responsibility boundaries, combining organization policies, delegated administrators, a common identity, centralized log aggregation, and exception approval.
choices.explanation: This achieves both separation and centralized control.

choices.text: Require all business units to use a single set of shared root credentials.
choices.explanation: This eliminates separation of responsibilities and auditability.

choices.text: To avoid controls, allow each business unit to delete its logs independently.
choices.explanation: This prevents investigation and auditing across the organization.

checkpoints.prompt: Before releasing infrastructure changes to production, we want to prevent violations involving public access settings, encryption, and logging settings. Which policy is most appropriate?

choices.text: Permanently disable the checks in preparation for emergencies.
choices.explanation: This eliminates the scope and expiration date of exceptions.

choices.text: Check the settings only after applying them to production.
choices.explanation: This could expose a noncompliant state.

choices.text: Validate IaC and artifacts within the delivery process, and stop violations before deployment except for approved, time-limited exceptions.
choices.explanation: This integrates protection into the delivery process.

checkpoints.prompt: A 7-day exception allowing TCP port 22 from the internet had been approved in the security group for a test EC2 instance. AWS Config detected that the rule was still present after the exception expired. The security team has confirmed that SSH access from the administrative network works. What is the appropriate action?

choices.text: Because the previous approval exists, suppress the finding even after the exception expires.
choices.explanation: The approval is valid only until its expiration. Suppressing the finding afterward could allow the publicly accessible rule to remain unintentionally.

choices.text: Review the current exception and rules, then use a least-privilege remediation to remove only the public TCP 22 rule from the target group. Afterward, recheck administrative connectivity and compliance status.
choices.explanation: This remediates only the target whose exception has expired and verifies that the public rule is gone while preserving the required administrative path.

choices.text: Delete all security group rules in the same account.
choices.explanation: This would also remove unrelated permissions, potentially blocking communications required for normal administration and business operations.
